intro: Many people help keep us well. Doctors check our bodies. Nurses give shots and answer questions. Dentists care for our teeth. Pharmacists get medicine ready.
Our feelings are part of our health too. In this unit you will learn what happens at a checkup. You will learn to name feelings and find ways to feel calm. You will learn who to ask for help.
bigQuestion: Who helps us stay well, and how can we help ourselves?

timeline.t: You check in at the doctor's office with a grown-up.
A nurse measures how tall you are.
You step on a scale to see your weight.
The doctor listens to your heart with a stethoscope.
The doctor looks in your ears with a small light.
You may get a shot that helps your body fight germs.
If you feel nervous, you take slow, calm breaths.
You ask your questions and say thank you.

words.d: a person who studied a long time to help keep bodies well
a helper who cares for sick people and checks how they are
a visit to the doctor to make sure you are well
a tool doctors use to listen to your heart and lungs
a shot or medicine that helps your body learn to fight a germ
a time when someone needs help right away
what is going on inside you, like happy, sad or mad
breathing in and out slowly to help your body relax

test.q: Who gets medicine ready at a drugstore?
test.why: A pharmacist gets medicine ready and explains how to use it.

test.q: What does a doctor use to hear your heart?
test.why: A stethoscope lets the doctor hear your heart.

test.q: What does a vaccine help your body do?
test.why: A vaccine helps your body learn to fight a germ.

test.q: What number do you call in an emergency?
test.why: 911 is the number for fast help.
Only take medicine from a trusted adult.

choices: A visit to make sure you are well
test.why: A checkup is a visit when you are not sick.

test.q: Which one is a body clue for worry?
test.why: A tight tummy is a body clue for worry.

test.q: How do you do calm breathing?
test.why: Calm breathing is slow breathing in and out.

test.q: Is it okay to feel nervous at the doctor?
choices: Yes, and you can ask questions
test.why: Feeling nervous is okay, and doctors like questions.

test.q: Who is a school helper for feelings?
test.why: A school counselor listens and helps kids with feelings.

write.prompt: Pretend a friend is nervous about a checkup. What would you tell your friend? Use two facts from this unit to help your friend feel brave.
tips: Name one helper and what they do.
Name one tool, like a stethoscope.
Share one way to feel calm.

title: Helpers Who Keep Us Well

chapters.title: A Visit to the Doctor
chapters.bigQuestion: How do helpers at the doctor's office keep us well?

story.title: Maya Hears Her Heart
story.kicker: Maya feels nervous at her checkup, until the nurse shares a special tool.
paragraphs: Maya sat on the paper-covered bed. The paper crinkled when she moved. Her tummy felt tight. She squeezed her dad's hand hard.
A nurse named Mr. Ruiz came in with a smile. He said, "It is okay to feel nervous. You can ask me anything." Maya asked, "What is that thing on your neck?"
"This is a stethoscope," said Mr. Ruiz. "It helps me hear your heart." He put the soft ends in Maya's ears. He held the round part on her chest.
Thump-thump. Thump-thump. Maya's eyes got big. "That is my heart!" she said. Her tummy did not feel so tight anymore.
story.think: What helped Maya feel less nervous at her checkup?

lessons.title: Doctors and Nurses
lessons.mainIdea: Doctors and nurses help us stay well and help us get better when we are sick.
reading: Think of a clinic near your home. A *doctor* works there. A doctor checks your body. A doctor helps you get better when you are sick.
A *nurse* works there too. Nurses check how you are doing. They give shots. They answer questions. Doctors and nurses work as a team.

words.d: a person who studied a long time to help keep bodies well
a helper who cares for sick people and checks how they are

look.title: A Busy Clinic
look.text: Picture a clinic. A nurse writes down a boy's height. A doctor looks in a girl's ears. A baby waits on her mom's lap.
look.prompt: Who is working as a team in this clinic?

check.q: Who helps you get better when you are sick?
check.why: A doctor checks your body and helps you get better.

check.q: What is one thing a nurse does?
check.why: The reading says nurses give shots and answer questions.

check.q: How do doctors and nurses work?
check.why: The reading says doctors and nurses work as a team.

lessons.title: Dentists and Pharmacists
lessons.mainIdea: Dentists care for teeth, and pharmacists give out medicine safely.
reading: A *dentist* looks at your teeth. The dentist counts them. The dentist cleans them. The dentist shows you how to brush well.
A *pharmacist* works in a drugstore. A pharmacist gets medicine ready. A pharmacist tells your family how to use it safely.

words.d: a doctor who cares for teeth and gums
a person who gets medicine ready and explains how to use it safely

look.title: Two Helpers
look.text: Look at two pictures. In one, a girl opens her mouth wide in a big chair. In the other, a man in a white coat hands a small bag across a counter.
look.prompt: Which picture shows a dentist? Which shows a pharmacist?

check.q: Who cares for your teeth?
check.why: A dentist is a doctor for teeth and gums.

check.q: Where does a pharmacist work?
check.why: The reading says a pharmacist works in a drugstore.

check.q: What does a pharmacist tell your family?
check.why: A pharmacist explains how to use medicine safely.

lessons.title: Growing Taller
lessons.mainIdea: At a checkup, a nurse measures how tall you are and how much you weigh.
reading: A *checkup* is a visit when you are not sick. It helps you stay well. First, you stand tall against a wall. The nurse measures your height.
Next, you step on a scale. It shows your weight. The doctor looks at these numbers each year. They show that you are growing.

words.d: a visit to the doctor to make sure you are well

look.title: Marks on the Wall
look.text: Look at a door frame at Sam's house. There is a pencil mark for age 4. A higher mark says age 5. The highest mark says age 6.
look.prompt: What do the marks tell you about Sam?

check.q: When do you have a checkup?
choices: Only when you are very sick
When you are well, to stay well
check.why: A checkup is a visit when you are not sick.

check.q: What does a scale show?
check.why: You step on a scale and it shows your weight.

check.q: Why does the doctor look at your height each year?
choices: To see that you are growing
check.why: The numbers show that you are growing.

lessons.title: Heart and Ears
lessons.mainIdea: The doctor uses tools to listen to your heart and look in your ears.
reading: The doctor uses a *stethoscope*. It has two ends for the ears and a round part. The round part goes on your chest. The doctor hears your heart beat.
Then the doctor uses a small light. It helps the doctor look inside your ears. Nothing goes in far. It does not hurt.

words.d: a tool doctors use to listen to your heart and lungs

look.title: Thump-Thump
look.text: Put your hand flat on your chest. Sit very still. Can you feel a soft thump-thump? That is your heart working.
look.prompt: What tool would help you hear your heart even better?

check.q: What does a stethoscope help the doctor do?
check.why: A stethoscope lets the doctor hear your heart beat.

check.q: Where does the round part of the stethoscope go?
check.why: The reading says the round part goes on your chest.

check.q: What does the doctor use to look in your ears?
check.why: The doctor uses a small light to look inside your ears.

lessons.title: Shots Help Us
lessons.mainIdea: Shots help your body learn to fight some germs.
reading: Sometimes you get a shot at a checkup. Many shots are *vaccines*. A vaccine helps your body learn to fight a germ.
A shot can pinch for a moment. You can hold a hand. You can take a big breath. Soon the pinch is gone, and your body is ready.

words.d: a shot or medicine that helps your body learn to fight a germ

look.title: Ready for a Shot
look.text: Picture Leo in the chair. His mom holds his hand. He looks at a poster of a fish. He breathes in slow and breathes out slow.
look.prompt: What things help Leo feel calm?

check.q: What does a vaccine do?
choices: Helps your body learn to fight a germ
check.why: A vaccine helps your body learn to fight a germ.

check.q: How long does a shot pinch?
check.why: The reading says a shot can pinch for a moment.

check.q: What can help you during a shot?
check.why: Holding a hand and big breaths can help.

lessons.title: Asking Questions
lessons.mainIdea: It is okay to feel nervous and to ask questions at the doctor.
reading: Many kids feel *nervous* at the doctor. Adults do too. That is okay. Feelings are part of being a person.
You can ask questions. You can say, "What is that?" or "Will it hurt?" Doctors and nurses like questions. Answers help you feel brave.

words.d: a worried feeling about something that is coming

look.title: Good Questions
look.text: Here are some questions kids ask. What is that tool? What will you do next? Will it hurt? Why do I need this?
look.prompt: What question would you like to ask a doctor?

check.q: Is it okay to feel nervous at the doctor?
check.why: The reading says many kids and adults feel nervous, and that is okay.

check.q: How do doctors feel about questions?
check.why: Doctors and nurses like questions.

check.q: What helps you feel brave?
check.why: The reading says answers help you feel brave.

lessons.title: Medicine From a Trusted Adult
lessons.mainIdea: Take medicine only when a trusted adult gives it to you.
reading: Medicine can help a sick body. But too much can hurt. Some pills look like candy. They are not candy.
Only take *medicine* from a trusted adult. That could be a parent, a grown-up at home or the school nurse. If you find pills, do not touch them. Tell an adult.

words.d: something that helps a sick body get better when used the right way
a grown-up who keeps you safe, like a parent or school nurse

look.title: Pills on the Floor
look.text: Ana sees small pink pills on the kitchen floor. They look like candy. Her grandpa is in the next room.

check.q: Who should give you medicine?
check.why: Only take medicine from a trusted adult.

check.q: What should you do if you find pills?
choices: Do not touch them and tell an adult
check.why: The reading says do not touch them and tell an adult.

check.q: Why is medicine not candy?
check.why: Medicine can help, but too much can hurt.

lessons.title: Calling 911
lessons.mainIdea: In an emergency, call 911 to get help fast.
reading: An *emergency* is when someone is badly hurt or in danger. It needs help right away. A fire is an emergency. A person who will not wake up is an emergency.
Call *911* on a phone. Stay calm. Say what is wrong. Say where you are. Stay on the phone until the helper says you can hang up.

words.d: a time when someone needs help right away
the phone number to call for fast help in an emergency

look.title: What to Say
look.text: The helper on the phone asks: What is wrong? Where are you? You answer: My grandma fell and will not wake up. We are at 12 Oak Street.
look.prompt: What two things did you tell the helper?

check.q: What number do you call in an emergency?
check.why: 911 is the number for fast help.

check.q: Which one is an emergency?
check.why: A fire needs help right away.

check.q: When can you hang up?
choices: When the helper says you can
check.why: Stay on the phone until the helper says you can hang up.

review.q: Who helps you take care of your teeth?
review.why: A dentist is a doctor for teeth and gums.

review.q: What tool lets you hear a heart?
review.why: A stethoscope lets you hear the heart beat.

choices: A visit to make sure you are well
review.why: A checkup is a visit when you are not sick.

review.q: In the story, what helped Maya feel better?
review.why: The nurse let Maya hear her heart, and her tummy felt less tight.
Only take medicine from a trusted adult.

review.q: What do you say when you call 911?
choices: What is wrong and where you are
review.why: Tell the helper what is wrong and where you are.

chapters.title: Feelings and Calm Bodies
chapters.bigQuestion: What can we do when big feelings show up in our bodies?

story.title: Balloon Breathing
story.kicker: Before a spelling test, Jamal's tummy feels tight, and his teacher shows him a trick.
paragraphs: It was Friday. Spelling test day. Jamal sat at his desk. His tummy felt tight, like a fist. His hands felt sweaty.
Ms. Lee knelt by his desk. "You look worried," she said softly. Jamal nodded. "My tummy feels funny." Ms. Lee said, "Let's try balloon breathing."
"Put your hands on your tummy," she said. "Breathe in slowly through your nose. Fill your tummy like a balloon. Now let the air out slowly."
Jamal did it three times. His tummy felt softer. His hands felt calm. He picked up his pencil. He was ready to try.
story.think: Where in his body did Jamal feel his worry?

lessons.title: Many Feelings
lessons.mainIdea: Everyone has many feelings, and we can name them.
reading: You wake up and it snows. You feel happy. Your friend moves away. You feel sad. Someone takes your toy. You feel mad.
A *feeling* is what is going on inside you. Happy, sad, mad, scared and worried are all feelings. Every feeling is okay to have.

words.d: what is going on inside you, like happy, sad or mad

look.title: Faces
look.text: Look at three faces. One has a big smile. One has tears on the cheeks. One has tight lips and a wrinkled forehead.
look.prompt: What feeling does each face show?

check.q: Your friend moves away. How might you feel?
check.why: The reading says you might feel sad when a friend moves away.

check.q: Which one is a feeling?
check.why: Worried is a feeling, like happy or scared.

check.q: Are all feelings okay to have?
check.why: The reading says every feeling is okay to have.

lessons.title: Scared and Worried
lessons.mainIdea: Being scared or worried is a way our body tries to keep us safe.
reading: A big dog barks. You jump back. You feel *scared*. Being scared can help you stay away from danger.
*Worried* is a feeling about something that might happen. You may worry about a test or a new class. Worry often gets smaller when you talk about it.

words.d: a feeling that something might hurt you
a feeling of thinking about something that might go wrong

look.title: First Day
look.text: It is Rosa's first day at a new school. She does not know anyone yet. She keeps thinking, What if nobody plays with me?
look.prompt: What feeling does Rosa have? Who could she talk to?

check.q: How can being scared help you?
choices: It helps you stay away from danger
check.why: Being scared can help you stay away from danger.

check.q: What is worry about?
check.why: Worry is a feeling about something that might happen.

check.q: What often makes worry smaller?
check.why: The reading says worry often gets smaller when you talk about it.

lessons.title: Body Clues
lessons.mainIdea: Feelings show up in our bodies, and we can notice the clues.
reading: Feelings do not stay only in your head. When you are mad, your face may get hot. When you are worried, your tummy may feel tight.
These are *body clues*. When you are scared, your heart may beat fast. Noticing a clue helps you know what you feel.

words.d: a sign in your body that shows a feeling, like a tight tummy

look.title: Where Do You Feel It?
look.text: Picture a boy at the top of a tall slide. His heart beats fast. His hands hold the rail tight. His legs feel wobbly.
look.prompt: What feeling might these body clues show?

check.q: When you are mad, what may happen to your face?
check.why: The reading says your face may get hot when you are mad.

check.q: In the story, where did Jamal feel his worry?
check.why: Jamal's tummy felt tight before the test.

check.q: Why is it good to notice body clues?
choices: They help you know what you feel
check.why: Noticing a clue helps you know what you feel.

lessons.title: Everyone's Brain Is Different
lessons.mainIdea: Every brain works in its own way, and that is okay.
reading: Your *brain* helps you think and feel. Every brain works in its own way. Some kids like quiet. Some kids like to move while they learn.
Loud sounds may bother one kid and not another. One kid may need a break. Another may need a hug. Knowing what helps you is a strength.

words.d: the part inside your head that helps you think, feel and move

look.title: Two Friends
look.text: At a birthday party, Ben laughs and jumps near the loud music. His friend Ava puts on soft earmuffs and sits in a quiet corner with a book.
look.prompt: What helps Ben? What helps Ava?

check.q: What does your brain help you do?
check.why: The reading says your brain helps you think and feel.

check.q: Do all brains work the same way?
choices: No, each works in its own way
check.why: Every brain works in its own way.

check.q: What is a strength?
check.why: The reading says knowing what helps you is a strength.

lessons.title: Calm Breathing
lessons.mainIdea: Slow breathing can help a body feel calm.
reading: Try this. Pretend to smell a flower. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Now pretend to blow out a candle. Breathe out slowly.
This is *calm breathing*. Slow breaths tell your body it is safe. Your heart can slow down. Your tummy can feel softer.

words.d: breathing in and out slowly to help your body relax

look.title: Flower and Candle
look.text: Hold up one finger like a flower. Smell it slowly. Now pretend your finger is a candle. Blow out the flame softly. Do it three times.
look.prompt: How does your body feel after three slow breaths?

check.q: In calm breathing, what do you pretend to smell?
check.why: You pretend to smell a flower as you breathe in.

check.q: How should you breathe out?
check.why: You breathe out slowly, like blowing out a candle.

check.q: What do slow breaths tell your body?
check.why: Slow breaths tell your body it is safe.

lessons.title: Stretching and Quiet Time
lessons.mainIdea: Stretching and quiet time can help a busy body rest.
reading: Reach your arms up high like a tall tree. Now bend and touch your toes. *Stretching* helps tight muscles let go.
*Quiet time* helps too. You can sit in a cozy corner. You can look at a book or listen to soft music. A few quiet minutes can help you feel ready again.

words.d: reaching and bending your body slowly to loosen your muscles
a few calm minutes to rest your body and mind

look.title: The Calm Corner
look.text: In one classroom there is a calm corner. It has a soft rug, two pillows, a basket of books and a small timer.
look.prompt: How could a kid use this corner to feel calm?

check.q: What does stretching help?
check.why: Stretching helps tight muscles let go.

check.q: What can you do in quiet time?
check.why: In quiet time you can look at a book or listen to soft music.

check.q: How can a few quiet minutes help?
choices: They help you feel ready again
check.why: The reading says quiet minutes can help you feel ready again.

lessons.title: Asking for Help
lessons.mainIdea: When a feeling is too big, ask a trusted adult for help.
reading: Sometimes a feeling is too big to handle alone. That is okay. You can ask for *help*.
Tell a trusted adult. That could be a parent, a teacher or the school counselor. You can say, "I feel worried. Can we talk?" Sharing a feeling can make it lighter.

words.d: support from someone when something is hard
a school helper who listens and helps kids with feelings

look.title: Who Can Help?
look.text: Make a list of grown-ups who help you. Maybe a mom or dad. Maybe a grandma. Maybe your teacher. Maybe the school counselor.
look.prompt: Who is one trusted adult you could talk to?

check.q: What can you do when a feeling is too big?
choices: Ask a trusted adult for help
check.why: The reading says you can ask a trusted adult for help.

check.q: Who is a school helper for feelings?
check.why: A counselor listens and helps kids with feelings.

check.q: What can sharing a feeling do?
check.why: Sharing a feeling can make it lighter.

lessons.title: Kindness Helps Everyone
lessons.mainIdea: Kind words and actions help everyone feel safe.
reading: Mia saw a boy sitting alone at lunch. She sat down and said, "Hi, want to share my grapes?" The boy smiled.
That was *kindness*. Kind words and actions help people feel safe. When we feel safe, our bodies feel calmer. Kindness helps the helper feel good too.

words.d: being friendly, caring and helpful to others

look.title: Kind or Not?
look.text: One kid laughs when a friend drops her tray. Another kid helps her pick it up and says, "That happens to everyone."
look.prompt: Which kid showed kindness? How might the friend feel?

check.q: What did Mia do that was kind?
choices: She sat with the boy and shared
check.why: Mia sat down and shared her grapes.

check.q: How do kind actions help people?
check.why: Kind words and actions help people feel safe.

check.q: Who feels good when you are kind?
choices: The helper and the other person
check.why: The reading says kindness helps the helper feel good too.

review.q: Which of these is a feeling?
review.why: Mad is a feeling, like happy, sad and scared.

choices: A sign in your body that shows a feeling
review.why: A body clue is a sign in your body, like a tight tummy.

review.q: What did Ms. Lee teach Jamal?
review.why: Ms. Lee showed Jamal balloon breathing before his test.

review.q: In calm breathing, you smell a flower and then...
review.why: You breathe out slowly, like blowing out a candle.
Every brain works in its own way, and that is okay.

review.q: Who can you ask for help with a big feeling?
review.why: A parent, teacher or counselor can help.
